quotes.text: The real learning curve isn't the grammar of the language, but the reasoning about probabilistic states, measurement, and interference.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Pinpoints where the actual difficulty of quantum programming lies.

quotes.text: Correctness isn't about identical outputs, but about whether your sequence of operations shapes the probability distribution exactly as anticipated.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Redefines correctness for developers coming from deterministic code.

quotes.text: Whenever you write a new operation, don't settle for one result. Run it many times on the simulator so you can validate that the distribution matches your understanding before sending the job to actual hardware.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: A concrete, actionable debugging practice for quantum code.

quotes.text: Rather than interpreting that as a logic bug, it's better to treat it as measured physical data.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Helps developers interpret noisy hardware results correctly.

quotes.text: Quantum programming isn't abstract wizardry. It's code you can write, run, and debug today. The syntax looks familiar, the tooling works inside editors you already use
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Summarises the episode's message that quantum development is approachable now.

chapters.title: Your quantum playground: setting up Q# and Azure Quantum
Debugging in a world where you can't peek

takeaways: Q# looks like a familiar language with namespaces, operations and types; the real shift is reasoning about qubits, probabilities, measurement and interference.
A working setup needs a current .NET SDK, the Quantum Development Kit with the Q# extension in VS Code, and an Azure subscription with a Quantum workspace linked through the Azure CLI.
Debug quantum programs statistically on the simulator with many shots and assertions, then treat deviations on real Azure Quantum hardware as physical noise rather than logic bugs.
hook: Quantum computing sounds like physics homework, but developers can write Q# on a laptop today. This episode walks .NET and cloud developers through setup, a first Hello World with a Hadamard gate, statistical debugging on the simulator and submitting the same job to Azure Quantum hardware.
